doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

chapter: Becoming an audio man and DJ
title: Quitting trumpet and turning to sound work
summary: He played trumpet in rock and soul bands, stopped for being out of tune, and became an audio man.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Okay. Well when you got to be 17, 18 thinking what kind of outlet is there for this passion I have—

Yeah. I thought about it a lot, surprisingly a lot. I scoped out what I wanted to do pretty quickly and stuck to it very seriously. I mean for a minute there I wanted to be a trumpet player. I got a trumpet and I practiced too much, as my neighbors I’m sure could tell you, and I got a little bit of facility in the upper register, but I played stupid. And I was smart enough to know I was playing stupid. When I played with rock & roll bands, you know, I just recently ran into this guy, he actually had a minor career in big time rock & roll, Lou Erlanger. I think he goes as Lou X. Erlanger. He was with Mink Deville and a couple of other things. But they had a band called the Stingrays. And I helped them. Because they were good. And they thought I was good. And they were wrong. And I’m still wondering what on earth — and I recently met Lou again for a jazz reason I’m pleased to say and you know he still remembers that he dug me. Because I swung better than they did, no offense, Lou and his band, the Stingrays. And they were encouraging me. But I was impressed at their facility on their instruments and their intonation. They were better on electric guitar than I was on trumpet, and they played in tune. I had an upper register on trumpet but I had a shrill tone and I got excited and I played woefully out of tune, sharp largely, which I can hear. Good enough to hear it, not good enough to stop. So I stopped playing. And the other reason why was because of my sound career. I made a few gigs at a place called the McGill House in Jamaica, Queens. This was — I mean from my point of view I mean I was doing nothing. We played, a trombone player, a tenor player and me, we’d play a chord behind some singer trying to be the next Diana Ross. She wasn’t that famous yet, there was just the Supremes. Or something like that. And that was the gig. And then downstairs — it was really actually a very well run operation. Downstairs they had like, it was more like Gerde’s Folk City. It wasn’t so much the hootenanny thing but the protest folk music thing which is a little more interesting to me, and then with like apple cider and donuts and people you could talk to

and I’m sure I was attracted to a couple of young females who I went to high school with down there. But I was playing with the rhythm & blues, or soul as it was starting to be called, upstairs. And the sound was good. And I used to talk to the sound guy. And then I’d go hear Roy Eldridge, that was say a Saturday night dance on Sunday I’d say, “Roy, you know the sound isn’t too good.” He said “I’m hip, tell me about it, please believe me I need help.” And gradually I became an audio guy. And this really, I think, triggered the idea of helping the musicians who deserve to be helped rather than becoming an undeserving musician. And that transition occurs over the late 60s and basically my Columbia college years. And I’m out of the trumpet business. Well I played Milestones at the West End on March 11, 1974 with Paul Quinichette and Matthew Gee, and Sam Woodyard. And I was playing Frank Williams’ horn so he wasn’t playing. I don’t know who was on piano. It might have been Frank Williams, he had good piano playing. Or that might have been it. There may have been no chordal root. But we were playing a modal piece so that makes sense. There was no chordal root. And then Gee and Quinichette, who pache, their souls were drunks, they laid out on the bridge you know, and I think there’s an E above the staff you’ve got to hit twice in the bridge [humms], there was just me out in the open, me and Woodyard. And I said I’ll never do that again in life. And I haven’t. I did play my notes right then, and so I said I’m batting a thousand, time to retire.
